passage:
I'm Chaitanya, and I was the odd one in that room. Four of us on the shortlist panel, and three had studied at the same engineering college. The candidate was Nirmala, sharp portfolio, from a college none of us knew. Someone said, “She may not fit our style.” Another said, “Rohit is from our place, we know how his batch works.” I said nothing that day. I'm not proud of it.

Afterwards I counted our last five hires: all from two colleges. What we called merit had a lot of comfort in it. Next round I asked, before anyone spoke, “What would we look for if these names weren't on the page?” Nobody argued. Nobody looked at me either. Nirmala got a second interview. I still wonder about the ones who never did.

qa.q: How many of the four panel members had studied at the same engineering college?
qa.a: Three of the four had studied at the same engineering college.

qa.q: Why is Chaitanya not proud of staying silent that day?
qa.a: Chaitanya saw a comfortable bias shaping the choice and did not speak, and that silence let Nirmala's chances shrink.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya do in the next round that changed how the panel talked?
qa.a: Chaitanya asked the panel what they would look for if the names were not on the page, before anyone spoke.

qa.q: What was the shortlist meeting like for Nirmala, though Nirmala was not in the room?
qa.a: Nirmala was judged on a college name rather than the portfolio, so a strong application risked being shut out quietly, unseen by Nirmala.

grounding: A panel member notices a hiring panel favouring its own college and quietly asks the panel to look past the names.

passage:
Imran here, from the analytics desk. I sit two desks from Vinita, so I saw how it went. In March she promoted Karthik, who'd studied at her old university. In April she hired two more from there. Then Tessa interviewed, top scores on the test, a degree from somewhere else, and the note said, “Not a culture fit.” I can't tell what Vinita really feels. She's kind, and I think she truly believes she picks the best person.

But three people in a row, same university. I asked whether we could review test scores before the interview chat. She paused, tapped her pen and said, “Maybe. I hadn't seen it that way.” I don't know yet if anything will change.

qa.q: Which university had Karthik studied at?
qa.a: Karthik had studied at Vinita's old university.

qa.q: What might Imran be feeling when asking about reviewing test scores?
qa.a: Imran seems uneasy about the pattern but careful and unsure, since Imran calls Vinita kind and still does not know if anything will change.

qa.q: What small step did Imran suggest that could change how candidates are compared?
qa.a: Imran suggested reviewing test scores before the interview chat, so scores are seen before any feeling of familiarity.

qa.q: How might Vinita see the last three people she chose?
qa.a: Vinita likely sees good people who fit easily, and probably believes each hire was the best on merit without noticing how familiar the background felt.

grounding: An observer at work sees that a colleague who hires and promotes keeps choosing people from her own university and gently asks for a step that widens the view.
